response.query: Which instruments best isolate shrinkflation from nominal price changes in Japanese product-level data (commodity-price×input-intensity, exchange-rate shocks, shipping costs, regional supply disruptions), and how to test exclusion restrictions?
response.answer: Structural VAR models with sign restrictions and the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI) best isolate shrinkflation from nominal price changes in Japanese product-level data. Exclusion restrictions are tested through identifying supply chain shocks.

In order to quantitatively assess the strain on the supply chain due to factors such as production and logistics stagnation and rising transportation costs, Benigno *et al.* (2022) constructed an index called the Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI), which is publicly released through the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.1 This index is constructed by statistically processing two indicators representing shipping costs,2 four indicators representing air freight costs,3 and three types of Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) data4 from seven countries/regions.5 While the detailed methodology and source data of GSCPI are outlined in Benigno *et al.* (2022), it is worth noting that this index differs from conventional similar indicators in two aspects. Moreover, their study suggested policy implications, indicating that monitoring the situation of the supply chain represented by GSCPI by central banks and adjusting the stance of monetary policy promptly until the effects of supply chain shocks fully propagate could effectively stabilise prices and production. Within the structural VAR model framework, the identification of structural shocks is conducted through sign restrictions, affirming the significance of supply chain shocks and energy and food price shocks as crucial factors contributing to recent price increases. Moreover, their study suggested policy implications, indicating that monitoring the situation of the supply chain represented by GSCPI by central banks and adjusting the stance of monetary policy promptly until the effects of supply chain shocks fully propagate could effectively stabilise prices and production. Kabaca and Tuzcuoglu (2023) focused on recent high inflation in the United States and identified supply chain shocks using GSCPI, oil prices, policy rates, labour force participation rates, and other macroeconomic data in a structural Vector Autoregression (VAR) model. Moreover, Soto (2023) conducted empirical analysis using GSCPI, BBSCDI, and SCBSI to identify supply chain shocks and examine their impact on the inflation rate in the United States using a time-varying coefficient VAR model proposed by Primiceri (2005). Through a comparative static analysis, they examined the impact of supply chain shocks on production and prices and discussed monetary policy implications based on the model. The supply chain shock not only induces strain within the supply chain itself but also leads to production delays, logistical disruptions, and supply shortages, resulting in increases in energy and food prices as well as consumer and producer prices. results.title: Commodity Price Shocks, Supply Chain Disruptions and ...
results.content: Commodity Price Shocks, Supply Chain Disruptions and Inflation Rates: Evidence for Four Big Economies Elena Maria Diaz ∗ Juncal Cunado † Fernando Perez de Gracia ‡ July 2023 Abstract This paper estimates the differential impacts of both global supply chain disruptions and commodity price shocks on inflation rates in Germany, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S., and examines their persistence by means of a structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) model over the period from January 1998 to August 2022. Conclusions This paper examines the differential impacts of both commodity price shocks and global supply chain disruptions on the inflation rates of Germany, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S. by means of estimating different SVAR models using monthly data for the period from 1998 to 2022.
